subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: disclosing quickly and owning it [Action]
passage:
Tuesday, 10:42. Preeti ran a cleanup command, saw the screen scroll, and felt the blood leave her face. The customer table in the live system was gone. She had typed it in the wrong window.
Four minutes later Preeti was at Eshaan's desk. "I deleted the customer table on the live system. I ran the cleanup at 10:42 in the wrong window. Everything since last night's backup is missing, I think, and I don't know about anything else."
Wednesday. Eshaan's team restored last night's backup by noon and rebuilt the day's entries from the logs by evening.
Friday. In the review, Eshaan said, "You telling us in four minutes gave us the whole day. Tell us the same way next time."

qa.q: At what time did Preeti run the cleanup command?
What was Preeti feeling when she saw the screen scroll?
qa.a: Preeti felt shock and dread, as the blood left her face when she realised the table was gone.

qa.q: What could the team do to make sure a slip like this is caught earlier?
qa.a: They could add a confirmation step and separate windows for test and live work, so one wrong window cannot erase live data.

qa.q: How might Eshaan have felt when Preeti arrived at the desk?
qa.a: Eshaan was probably alarmed but grateful for the clear, immediate report, which let the team start work at once.

grounding: The passage shows an engineer who deletes a customer table by mistake, tells the lead within minutes with exact details and helps start recovery straight away.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: disclosing quickly and owning it [Action]
passage: Nandini, you look like you've broken something. Sit. Your Thomas sir broke something much bigger once. I was twenty-four, in my second month on the database team. One Friday evening I ran a cleanup script on what I thought was the test server. It was production. The customer table, gone. My hands went cold. For maybe thirty seconds I thought, nobody knows yet, maybe I can fix it quietly. Then I picked up the phone and called my lead, Mrs Iyer. I said, 'I've deleted the customer table on production at 6.42. This is the script. These three services are affected.' She didn't shout. She said, 'Good, now we know exactly where to start.' We restored from the backup by midnight. Twelve orders had to be re-entered by hand. If I'd waited till Monday, it would have been twelve thousand.

qa.q: At what time did Thomas delete the customer table?
What did Thomas feel in the first thirty seconds after the mistake?
qa.a: He felt cold panic and was tempted to hide it, thinking maybe he could fix it quietly.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Thomas's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Picking up the phone and telling Mrs Iyer exactly what happened, because recovery started at once and only twelve orders were lost instead of thousands.

qa.q: How might Mrs Iyer have seen Thomas's call?
qa.a: She likely valued the clear, fast report, since knowing the script and affected services told her exactly where to start.

grounding: It shows a young engineer who deletes a customer table by mistake telling the lead within minutes, with exact details, so recovery starts at once.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: disclosing quickly and owning it [Action]
passage:
At 11.50 p.m., during a late migration, Sarika pressed Enter and watched the customer table in production disappear. Her lead, Manoj, was on a flight to Singapore, phone off. The office was empty except for the security guard.
Her heart was thudding, but she didn't close the laptop. By 11.54 she had posted in the incident channel and called the on-call manager listed under Manoj's name: 'I deleted the customer table in production at 11.50 by running the cleanup script against the wrong server. About forty thousand customer records. Orders placed since 9 p.m. may not be in the last backup.' She pasted the exact command.
The on-call manager was online in six minutes, and they started the restore at 12.10. When Manoj landed, he read the thread from top to bottom and sent one line: 'Thank you for telling us so fast.'

qa.q: What time did Sarika delete the customer table?
qa.a: At 11.50 p.m., during a late migration.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling after pressing Enter, and how did she act despite it?
qa.a: Her heart was thudding with fear, but she stayed at the laptop and reported it within four minutes.

qa.q: What else could the team add so a missing lead isn't a problem next time?
qa.a: A clear on-call list and a short template for reporting incidents, so anyone can give the same details quickly.

qa.q: How might Manoj feel reading the thread after landing?
qa.a: Manoj is probably relieved and grateful that the problem was reported and handled while he couldn't be reached.

grounding: It shows an engineer who deletes production data at night reporting within minutes, explaining exactly what happened and which data is affected so recovery can begin.
